name: Tomas Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas, 58, and I help with wiring and repairs while the qualified electrician assigns and checks my tasks. I left night print work after saving for a change and took a vocational certificate; I'm still a junior, below the experienced workers for speed and skill, with no electrician's licence or sign-off authority. This firm pays above the usual rate, my partner books appointments for a window installer, and we have eleven months of expenses saved, grown children living elsewhere and a mortgage on our flat. There are plenty of electrical firms nearby, and I use AI occasionally for a checked note after a colleague has shown the tool works; retirement is a question I want real figures for, not an income I've confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the useful bits can stay without making every beginner learn a new slogan. I use AI occasionally for a short work note after a colleague has shown me the tool, then the senior checks it. I'd still rather understand the drawing than have the smoothest sentence about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages cover the mortgage and normal bills, with eleven months of expenses saved. The firm pays above the usual rate, and there are plenty of electrical employers nearby. I'm still junior, but this mild picture doesn't make me fear for our living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid supervised tasks actually offered. Starting now I'd keep a paper list of questions from each job and ask the senior about one unclear point during the paid shift before repeating the task. Through the first year we'd budget the actual two wages, counting no unconfirmed retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household, with the ordinary frustration of being slow at something new. I can enjoy getting a fitting in the right place after asking for help. I don't have to turn a good bank balance into a claim that I'm a good electrician already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What brought you into the trade at 58?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left night print work after saving for a change and completed a vocational certificate. I'm now a junior, below the experienced workers for skill and speed, with tasks assigned and checked by a qualified electrician. I don't have an electrician's licence or authority to approve an installation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who shares the household plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner books appointments for a window installer, and our children are grown and living elsewhere. We still have a mortgage on our flat. Retirement is something I'd like to understand soon, but I haven't confirmed the income, eligibility or dates that would let us stop relying on wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the booking part sounds a lot like my partner's working day. I'd want the employer to say what paid hours changed, not just how quickly an appointment could appear. At my firm I'd try a new tool once somebody could show it on work we understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own helper days could shrink if quicker planning meant fewer people on the job, and my partner's booking hours are more directly exposed. Eleven months saved gives us room to check a choice. It doesn't make either lost wage unimportant or make me skilled enough to replace it with higher electrical pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request three paid practice sessions with the approved AI note-sorting tool after a colleague demonstrated it on completed jobs. I'd take part only with no personal fee, normal weekly pay and hours retained, and qualified checking before any draft was used on actual work. In the first year I'd keep supervised tasks and review both actual wages with my partner each month, without choosing the partner's next career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household earnings, while still willing to try a proven aid. I'd rather admit both feelings than prove my cheerfulness at my partner's expense. A useful tool doesn't ask which wage we can afford to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the sorting tool changed a job detail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the example and show the original note to the qualified electrician. I wouldn't turn a suggestion into an instruction or a test result. The senior would still decide whether the record fitted the actual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm wanted unpaid practice at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid slot or stay with the existing checked method. I can afford some choices, but required learning is still part of the firm's work. I'd want the worker with no reserve to be able to use the same offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes at 60 in 2028, then capable robots around 63 in 2031. The booking wage at home faces the first date, not the extra physical-work interval. I'd keep asking for paid work and usable teaching, rather than tell older people a birthday had already solved their income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of my partner's booking wage to go in 2028, before robots could remove many junior helper tasks. My higher wage and eleven-month reserve help, but neither confirms how long we could cover the mortgage after both incomes changed. I'd be awake doing the sums before the retirement figures had even arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in spring 2027 in the short drawing-reading course only after the senior confirmed it fitted my assigned work, with total costs within 180 total spare wages, no lost pay and the eleven-month reserve untouched. I'd request branch budget help to check real retirement eligibility, amounts and start dates, subject to availability rather than an assumed appointment. In 2029 I'd take only actually offered paid supervised work within my physical ability, using completed teaching without claiming a licence or a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected booking-wage loss and the later physical risk. I can make one small learning choice without pretending it's a rescue for two incomes. I'd want the course to help me read today's drawing, not sell me an imaginary job at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the class cost more or took paid work time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait rather than use the reserve or lose wages to enrol. The 180 is the limit for all costs, not just the advertised fee. The senior would need to endorse the practical use before I chose it, and completed study would still leave the task supervised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does asking about retirement mean you can stop at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd need actual eligibility, amounts and payment dates against the household costs, with my partner agreeing any stopping plan. My grown children aren't a wage I can put beside the mortgage. I'd count only the confirmed figures before deciding anything.

His **first expected loss** is booking income in 2028; later work requires real paid offers, supervision and capacity, not an assumed pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us get real figures and learn something useful before the hardest change. Thinking AI arrives at 63 in 2031, then robots around 66 in 2034. I'd still want paid routes for the person who couldn't use savings to wait for an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra years help us compare actual choices, but I still expect the booking wage to face a large loss in 2031. That's a household worry even while my own current physical work continues. I don't know what retirement income would cover us or whether I'd have the health and an offer to work at 64.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the same senior-endorsed drawing course in spring 2027 only within 180 total spare wages, with no lost pay and the existing reserve untouched. I'd request available branch advice for actual income records while keeping only currently offered paid supervised tasks within my ability. In 2032 my partner and I would review confirmed resources and actual capacity before choosing real paid options or any exit, with an exit only if affordable and agreed by both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the expected booking-wage gap, though five years gives us more checking time. I'd still lie awake over the mortgage until real figures showed what could cover it. I can learn now without promising the site a working body forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your course make you qualified to work alone by 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short drawing class isn't an electrician's licence. I'd still need tasks within my actual skill and whatever qualified checks the job required. Being 64 doesn't turn a course receipt into sign-off authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the branch to help people without your money obtain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid teaching, clear hours and actual wages during a change, not an invitation to borrow first. I'd support a shared request during free time without missing paid shifts. I'd count no employer agreement or public funding before actual terms were confirmed.

Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to ask better questions without claiming one stopping age suits everyone. Thinking AI comes at 68 in 2036 and robots around 71 in 2039. I'd want our grown children to see a plan based on facts, not assume their father could work wherever the numbers needed him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own physical wage looks secure over the next few years, but the booking side of our household could be pressured before the full change. Eleven months saved means time to check, not an answer for the rest of our lives. I don't know what income, health or real paid options we'd have by 2037.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the endorsed drawing course in spring 2027 only within the same 180 spare wages, with no lost pay and the reserve untouched. We'd request available branch advice and review actual household records yearly, while I kept only offered paid supervised tasks within my current ability. In 2037 we'd use confirmed resources and actual capacity, considering an exit only if affordable and agreed with my partner, not assuming either a physical job at 69 or retirement payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possible earlier booking-income loss, with less urgency about distant full AGI. I'd like room to enjoy learning and our grown children's visits. I don't need a promise that I'll still be on a ladder at 69 to make today's work worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you expect the grown children to fund a shortfall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd count only help they'd actually offered and could manage, not their wages or a spare room I hadn't asked about. They have their own lives and future costs. I'd rather show them the real figures than call my wishes a family obligation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the later budget didn't support stopping or any work you could manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd take that actual shortfall to available advice and ask what support eligibility could be checked, without counting approval first. I wouldn't invent a wage because the plan needed one. A longer warning should let us name the gap honestly, not hide it inside the word retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect booking income to fall in 2028 before robots around 2031 also reach junior helper work. Clear paid hours, practical learning and actual income records would help. I'd want the same usable choices open to someone who couldn't pay for a class from spare wages or wait through uncertainty on savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether paying for a small course means somebody has funded a new career. My course budget buys a lesson, not a replacement for two household wages. I want to learn something useful without lending a certificate powers it doesn't have.

headlineQuote: My course budget buys a lesson, not a replacement for two household wages.
portrait: **Tomas, 58**, entered junior supervised work after night printing, with a vocational certificate, below-average practical skill and no electrician's licence or authority.
He has **higher pay**, eleven months saved, plenty of local firms, a booking-worker partner, grown children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI occasionally** after demonstration, while the partner's thinking-heavy bookings expose household income before later physical robots.
His **drawing-course choice** requires senior endorsement, an all-in 180 spare-wage limit, no lost pay and an untouched reserve without guaranteed later work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens booking wages before robots around 2031 reach helper tasks, while future retirement resources remain unconfirmed.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **paid hours** and practical learning would help maintain a usable route through change.
Actual **income records** with eligibility, amounts and dates would support decisions without assuming savings, child payments or automatic pensions close the gap.
